gap: No result ChatGPT got says how much power an attached extender takes from the laptop. From maker-side figures, the Trio 3 Pro draws 11 W, so on its own it would drain a 13-inch MacBook Air's 53.8 Wh battery in about 4.9 hours. The 4.5 W Duex Max would take about 12 hours.
standout_why: I opened all three pages ChatGPT cited. itechguides' '15 Best Laptop Screen Extenders for 2026' quotes only charger pass-through ratings (60 W, 65 W) and has no draw figures or derived numbers. Its hinge advice is qualitative ('Nearly three pounds attached... can change the hinge balance'). Macworld's 'Best Portable Monitors for Mac 2026' gives weights (Trio 3 Pro 4.13 lb, Duex Float 2 Pro 2.9 lb) but no power draw, no comparison with the laptop's weight and no battery maths. It also lists the Trio 3 Pro as 2× 1920×1080, while Chip.pl gives 2240×1400. The RTINGS portable page returned only navigation and named no extender. TechRadar's KYY X90E review, an uncited result, gives a 15 W adapter rating but no draw. So weight is partly covered by Macworld, but nothing covers screen power as a share of a named laptop's battery.
decides: This confirms the Trio 3 Pro as the pick for two added screens, but as a plug-in setup. At 11 W it outlasts a 13-inch MacBook Air M5 battery after about 4.9 hours, and it weighs about 1.55 times that laptop. For working on battery, the single-screen Duex Max (4.5 W, about 12 hours) and the stacked Duex Float 2 Pro (2.9 lb, about 1.07 times the laptop) win that segment. A shopper who will work unplugged should pick a single added screen, or carry power for the triple.

findings.label: Power draw in use (maker figure as printed by reviewer)
findings.source_title: Chip.pl, Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro test / recenzja
findings.note: Chip.pl's spec table says 'Pobór mocy podczas pracy: 11 W' (power draw in operation), energy class E, PD up to 65 W. This is a listed figure, not one Chip.pl measured. Chip.pl also says peak brightness is limited when the screens run only on laptop power.

findings.label: Weight (whole set, both screens)
findings.source_title: Chip.pl, Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro test / recenzja
findings.note: 'Całość waży około 1,9 kg' (the whole set weighs about 1.9 kg). 1.9 × 2.2046 = 4.19 lb. Macworld lists 4.13 lb (1.9 kg), so the two agree.

findings.label: Hours to drain a 13-inch MacBook Air M5 battery from the screens alone
findings.note: 53.8 Wh ÷ 11 W (Chip.pl) = 4.9 h. This ignores the laptop's own draw, so real runtime is shorter. On the 15-inch Air: 66.5 Wh ÷ 11 W = 6.0 h.

findings.label: Weight compared with a 13-inch MacBook Air M5
findings.note: 4.19 lb (Chip.pl 1.9 kg) ÷ 2.7 lb (Apple) = 1.55. Against the 15-inch Air: 4.19 ÷ 3.3 = 1.27.

findings.source_title: Chip.pl, Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro test / recenzja

findings.label: Power consumption (maker spec page)
findings.source_title: Mobile Pixels, Duex Max technical specification
findings.note: The page lists 14.1-inch, 1920×1080, 300 nit, 60 Hz and 'Power consumption: 4.5 W'. Its title says Duex Max without 'DS'. The panel specs match our DS record, but the page does not name the DS, and it lists no weight.

findings.label: Hours to drain a 13-inch MacBook Air M5 battery from the screen alone
findings.note: 53.8 Wh ÷ 4.5 W (Mobile Pixels spec page) = 12.0 h. On the 15-inch Air: 66.5 ÷ 4.5 = 14.8 h. Over an 8-hour day: 4.5 × 8 = 36 Wh, which is 67% of the 13-inch battery. The Trio 3 Pro would need 11 × 8 = 88 Wh, or 1.64 of those batteries.

findings.note: TechRadar gives 2.2 kg and 2× 1920×1080 over one USB-C cable (DP Alt Mode, no driver). 2.2 × 2.2046 = 4.85 lb ÷ 2.7 = 1.80. 4.15 MP ÷ 4.85 lb = 0.86 MP/lb. The 15 W adapter is a supply rating, not a measured draw.

findings.label: Laptop reference figures used in the arithmetic
findings.value: 13-inch MacBook Air (M5): 53.8 Wh, 2.7 lb; 15-inch: 66.5 Wh, 3.3 lb; up to two external displays
findings.note: The current Air is M5 and Apple lists up to two external displays. The spec page does not say whether that holds with the lid open.
